def: An oral iron chelator that binds excess iron for fecal excretion. It treats chronic iron overload from repeated transfusions and can cause kidney and liver toxicity.
A microscope with a bright adjustable slit of light used to examine the cornea, anterior chamber, iris and lens. It detects cells and flare in uveitis and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Small bile channels within the liver that collect bile from hepatocytes and merge into the left and right hepatic ducts. They are targeted in primary biliary cholangitis.
The ducts outside the liver that carry bile to the duodenum: the common hepatic duct, cystic duct and common bile duct. Obstruction causes cholestasis and jaundice.
Synthetic testosterone derivatives that build muscle. Misuse causes testicular atrophy, infertility, acne, gynecomastia in men, liver tumors and low HDL.
The artery supplying oxygenated blood to the liver, arising from the celiac trunk. It supplies about 25% of liver blood flow, with the portal vein providing the rest.
The antigen-specific immune response mediated by T and B lymphocytes. It is slower than innate immunity and generates memory.
Receptors on lymphocytes that recognize antigens: the T-cell receptor and the B-cell receptor (membrane immunoglobulin). Their diversity comes from V(D)J recombination.

A vaccine against Neisseria meningitidis, using capsular polysaccharide conjugates or protein antigens for serogroup B. It is given to adolescents, asplenic patients and those with complement deficiencies.
An immune-complex reaction in which antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissues and activate complement. Examples are serum sickness, lupus nephritis and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Pattern-recognition receptors on innate immune cells that detect microbial molecules. For example, TLR4 recognizes lipopolysaccharide, triggering NF-kB activation and cytokine release.
A Gram-negative rod that makes a red pigment at room temperature. It causes nosocomial infections such as pneumonia and urinary tract infections.
The receptor on T cells for IL-2; its alpha chain is CD25. Regulatory T cells express CD25, and signaling drives T-cell proliferation.
A receptor on T and NK cells that binds IL-12, promoting Th1 differentiation and interferon-gamma. Defects cause susceptibility to mycobacterial infections.

An antiphospholipid antibody that, with lupus anticoagulant and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I, defines antiphospholipid syndrome. It causes thromboses and recurrent miscarriage, and can give a false-positive VDRL.
A scratch of the corneal epithelium causing eye pain, tearing, photophobia and foreign body sensation. Fluorescein staining shows an epithelial defect; treatment is topical antibiotics.
An inherited TP53 mutation causing early-onset sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, leukemia and adrenocortical carcinoma. Inheritance is autosomal dominant.
The fibrous sleeve enclosing a synovial joint, lined by synovial membrane that makes lubricating fluid. It stabilizes the joint and is thickened in adhesive capsulitis.
An MHC class II allele associated with rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes.
Separation of the nail plate from the nail bed. Causes include psoriasis, fungal infection, trauma and thyroid disease.
Delayed muscle relaxation after contraction, such as difficulty releasing a handshake. It occurs in myotonic dystrophy and myotonia congenita.
A cadherin protein in desmosomes that holds keratinocytes together. Autoantibodies cause pemphigus vulgaris (desmoglein 3) and pemphigus foliaceus (desmoglein 1).
The oily secretion of sebaceous glands that lubricates skin and hair. Its overproduction and plugging of follicles contribute to acne.
A topical agent for acne that kills Cutibacterium acnes through oxidation and has mild keratolytic effects.
Persistent infection with hepatitis C virus, lasting over 6 months, usually silent for years. It leads to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma and is now curable with direct-acting antivirals.
The ring-shaped cartilage at the lower larynx, the only complete ring around the airway. It lies at C6 and is the point of pressure in Sellick maneuver.
An agent applied to living tissue to kill or inhibit microbes, such as chlorhexidine or alcohol. It differs from a disinfectant, which is used on objects.
Rapidly spreading muscle necrosis from Clostridium perfringens, producing gas in tissue (crepitus). Its alpha toxin is a lecithinase that lyses cells.
Interferon-alpha and -beta, secreted by virus-infected cells. They induce an antiviral state by activating RNase L and protein kinase R.
A heat-stable toxin from reef fish that opens sodium channels. It causes gastrointestinal illness and neurologic symptoms such as reversal of hot and cold sensation.
A chelator (British anti-Lewisite) that binds arsenic, mercury and lead. It is given by injection and can cause hypertension and pain at the site.
Use of heat or electric current to burn tissue, to stop bleeding or remove tissue.
Sudden severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs, suggesting a condition needing urgent evaluation or surgery, such as perforation or appendicitis.
Complete displacement of the tibia relative to the femur from high-energy trauma. It risks injury to the popliteal artery and common peroneal nerve.
Abnormal contraction of the sphincter at the ampulla of Vater, causing biliary-type pain or pancreatitis without gallstones.
An IV fluid of small dissolved salts and sugars, such as normal saline or lactated Ringer, used for volume resuscitation.
Permanent flexion deformity of the hand and wrist from forearm muscle ischemia, usually after compartment syndrome or supracondylar humerus fracture.
Imaging of the urinary tract with contrast. Intravenous pyelography shows the kidneys, ureters and bladder.
A branch of the lumbar plexus (L2-L4) that passes through the obturator foramen. It supplies thigh adductors and medial thigh skin.
Early extra heartbeats from atrial or ventricular foci. Premature ventricular beats have wide QRS and are usually benign.
Infusion of a recombinant enzyme to treat lysosomal storage diseases such as Gaucher and Fabry disease.
Surgical or catheter-based removal of an embolus from a blood vessel to restore flow.
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction due to impaired ventricular relaxation and filling. It is common in hypertension, diabetes and aging, and gives a stiff left ventricle and S4.
syn: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

def: A prostaglandin F2-alpha analog that causes uterine contraction. It treats postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony and can cause bronchospasm.
Bloody diarrhea from Entamoeba histolytica, spread by fecal-oral route. Trophozoites invade the colon (flask-shaped ulcers) and can cause liver abscess.
The genus of lice, including head and body lice. Body lice transmit Rickettsia prowazekii (epidemic typhus), Bartonella quintana (trench fever) and Borrelia recurrentis.
Reduced skin color from decreased melanin or melanocytes. Causes include vitiligo, albinism and postinflammatory change.
A genus of dermatophyte fungi that cause tinea of skin, hair and nails. Microsporum infections fluoresce under Wood lamp.
Signs of meningeal irritation (neck stiffness, Kernig and Brudzinski signs) without actual meningeal infection. It is seen in meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Long-chain fatty acids in mycobacterial cell walls that make them acid-fast and resistant to drying. Isoniazid blocks their synthesis.
The toxic component of Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin). It activates TLR4, causing fever, hypotension and septic shock.
Dormant, heat-resistant forms made by Bacillus and Clostridium in harsh conditions. They contain dipicolinic acid and survive boiling.
A painless, indurated ulcer of primary syphilis at the site of inoculation. It contrasts with the painful ulcer of chancroid.
Tertiary syphilis affecting the aorta, producing syphilitic aortitis with ascending aortic aneurysm and aortic regurgitation. Endarteritis of vasa vasorum is the mechanism.
A lipid layer derived from host cell membrane that surrounds some viruses. It carries viral glycoproteins and makes viruses sensitive to detergents.
A virus whose RNA genome can serve directly as mRNA and be translated. Examples include coronaviruses, picornaviruses and flaviviruses.
An HIV drug that blocks the CCR5 co-receptor, preventing viral entry into cells. It is used only for CCR5-tropic virus.
Dysfunction of the sinoatrial node causing bradycardia, pauses, and alternating fast and slow rhythms (tachy-brady syndrome). It presents with dizziness or syncope and is treated with a pacemaker.
Bloodstream infection in newborns. Early onset is usually group B Streptococcus or E. coli, and late onset includes Staphylococcus and Listeria.
Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis without symptoms or contagiousness. Tests are positive (PPD or interferon-gamma assay) with a normal chest x-ray; treatment prevents reactivation.
An aminoglycoside that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and causes misreading of mRNA. It is used for tuberculosis and can cause ototoxicity.
Skin or organ disease from migrating animal parasite larvae. Cutaneous form (hookworm) causes serpiginous itchy tracks, and visceral and ocular forms follow Toxocara infection.
A recombinant vaccine of hepatitis B surface antigen. It is given to infants and at-risk adults, leading to anti-HBs antibodies.
The main type of human immunodeficiency virus worldwide, a retrovirus that infects CD4 T cells. It causes AIDS.
The big toe. Hallux valgus is a bunion, and hallux rigidus is stiffness from osteoarthritis.
Resistance of a microbe or tumor to multiple unrelated drugs. In bacteria it arises from efflux pumps and plasmids, and in cancer from P-glycoprotein efflux.
An acute infection of an eyelid gland, usually Staphylococcus aureus, forming a tender red lump. External forms are called styes.
Pain and dysfunction of the jaw joint and chewing muscles, with clicking or limited opening.
A collection of pus between the tonsil and its capsule, a complication of tonsillitis. It causes unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice and deviation of the uvula.
The floor of the cranial cavity, divided into anterior, middle and posterior fossae. Fractures here cause CSF leak, raccoon eyes and Battle sign.
A cationic peptide antibiotic that disrupts Gram-negative outer membranes like a detergent. It is topical or reserved for resistant infections because of nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
A needle-like apparatus by which Gram-negative bacteria inject effector proteins directly into host cells. Salmonella, Shigella and Yersinia use it.
A live attenuated vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella, given at 12-15 months and 4-6 years. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency.
Immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold and redissolve on warming. They cause cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, associated with hepatitis C.
A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor for HIV (d4T), now rarely used due to pancreatitis, lactic acidosis and neuropathy.
A bacterial enzyme in folate synthesis that joins PABA to pteridine. It is inhibited by sulfonamides.
A sulfonamide antibiotic that inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, usually combined with trimethoprim. It can cause rash, hyperkalemia and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
A nitrosourea alkylating drug that crosses the blood-brain barrier, used for brain tumors. It can cause pulmonary fibrosis and myelosuppression.
A nitrosourea alkylating drug that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is used for brain tumors. Toxicity includes delayed myelosuppression.
A chemotherapy drug that inhibits topoisomerase I, causing DNA breaks. It is used in ovarian and small cell lung cancer and causes myelosuppression.
A topoisomerase I inhibitor used in colorectal cancer. Its toxicities are severe diarrhea and myelosuppression.
A tyrosine kinase inhibitor that blocks BCR-ABL and SRC kinases. It treats Philadelphia chromosome-positive leukemias and can cause pleural effusion.
A multi-target tyrosine kinase inhibitor blocking VEGF and PDGF receptors. It treats renal cell carcinoma and GIST, with hypertension as a toxicity.
An echinocandin antifungal that inhibits beta-glucan synthase in the fungal cell wall. It treats invasive candidiasis.
A fungal enzyme that converts flucytosine into 5-fluorouracil, the active antifungal. Human cells lack it.
The stage of the malaria parasite released from infected liver cells or red cells that invades red cells. Their release causes the fever cycle.
A nematode with a life cycle that includes autoinfection, so it can persist for decades. Larvae penetrate skin, causing diarrhea and cough, and can disseminate under immunosuppression.
The guinea worm, a nematode acquired by drinking water containing infected copepods. The adult female emerges through a painful skin blister.
A fluid-filled cyst from Echinococcus granulosus, usually in the liver, acquired from dog feces. Rupture can cause anaphylaxis.
A blood fluke with snail hosts that causes intestinal and hepatic schistosomiasis. Lateral-spined eggs lodge in the liver, causing periportal fibrosis.
Severe pancreatitis with death of pancreatic tissue. It can become infected, causing sepsis and organ failure.
Congenital blockage of the posterior nasal passage, bony or membranous. It causes respiratory distress in newborns, who are obligate nose breathers, and can be part of CHARGE syndrome.
Involuntary repetitive actions such as lip smacking, occurring during focal impaired-awareness seizures.
Overuse injury causing lateral knee pain from friction of the iliotibial band over the femoral epicondyle, common in runners.
Retinal vessel damage from chronic hypertension, with arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, hemorrhages and papilledema.
The duct of the submandibular gland, opening at the sublingual caruncle beside the frenulum. Stones commonly block it.
Zoonotic infection by Brucella from unpasteurized dairy or livestock contact. It causes undulating fever, sweats and arthritis.
Infection by Francisella tularensis from ticks, rabbits or aerosols. It causes ulcers and swollen lymph nodes or pneumonia and needs cysteine to grow.
Epidemic pleurodynia, caused by coxsackie B virus, with sudden severe pleuritic chest and abdominal pain and fever.
Coxsackie A virus infection in children causing fever and small vesicles on the posterior oropharynx and soft palate.
An inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor that blocks release of influenza A and B from cells. It can cause bronchospasm.
An antiviral that blocks the influenza A M2 ion channel, preventing uncoating. Resistance is now widespread.
Viral infection from a rodent-borne arenavirus (house mouse), presenting as aseptic meningitis. It can cause congenital hydrocephalus and chorioretinitis.
An arenavirus carried by rodents and transmitted by mouse excreta. It causes aseptic meningitis and congenital infection.
A herpesvirus infecting T cells in childhood, related to roseola infantum.
Needle aspiration of joint fluid for analysis. It diagnoses septic arthritis and crystal arthritis.
An inhaled mixture of epinephrine isomers that constricts airway vessels and reduces swelling. It treats croup and postextubation stridor.
A benign, ovarian nodule of luteinized cells arising in pregnancy, resolving postpartum. It may cause maternal virilization.
Envenomation by black widow spiders, with alpha-latrotoxin causing neurotransmitter release. It produces severe muscle cramps and abdominal rigidity.
Passing light through tissue to assess content. A scrotal mass that transilluminates is fluid-filled, as in hydrocele.
An acute-phase protein made by the liver in response to IL-6. It rises with inflammation and is used to monitor infection and cardiovascular risk.
The longest vein in the body, running up the medial leg. The great saphenous vein is harvested for bypass grafts and is involved in varicose veins.
Anesthetic injected into the epidural space to block nerve roots. It is used in labor, and complications include hypotension and dural puncture headache.
Transient painless monocular vision loss, like a curtain falling, from retinal emboli of carotid disease or ocular artery embolus.
Calcification and thrombosis of small dermal and fat vessels causing painful skin necrosis, mostly in end-stage kidney disease.
A synthetic glucocorticoid used topically, by injection into joints and intralesionally in keloids.
A fracture where a tendon or ligament pulls off a piece of bone at its attachment, common in adolescents.
Breast pain, often cyclical and related to hormonal changes. It can occur with fibrocystic change.
A fluid-filled cyst near the fallopian tube from embryologic remnants (the hydatid of Morgagni), usually benign.
A topical antimicrobial for burns, combining silver with a sulfonamide. It can cause leukopenia and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Placement of small tubes through the eardrum to ventilate the middle ear. It treats recurrent otitis media with effusion.
A topical immune response modifier that activates TLR7 to induce interferons. It treats genital warts, actinic keratosis and basal cell carcinoma.
A flexible or rigid tube with a camera used to view the airways and take biopsies or lavage.
The most common ovarian cancer, from surface epithelium, including serous and mucinous types. It is associated with BRCA mutations and elevated CA-125.
An abnormal tangle of vessels connecting arteries directly to veins without capillaries. Cerebral AVMs can cause hemorrhage or seizures.
Multiple adjacent rib fractures creating a free-moving chest wall segment that moves paradoxically with breathing. Underlying pulmonary contusion causes hypoxia.
Imaging of the bladder after filling it with contrast, used to find bladder rupture or reflux.
A neurologic score of consciousness from 3 to 15 based on eye, verbal and motor responses.
A hernia through a prior surgical scar in the abdominal wall.
Removal of uterine contents by vacuum aspiration, used for abortion and molar pregnancy.
An ergot alkaloid that causes sustained uterine contraction. It treats postpartum hemorrhage and is contraindicated in hypertension.
Leakage of urine with coughing or exertion because of weak pelvic floor or urethral sphincter support.
An abnormal connection between the bladder and vagina causing continuous urine leakage. It follows gynecologic surgery or obstructed labor.
A chronic inflammatory disease of apocrine gland areas, with painful nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts and scarring in the axillae and groin.
Inflammation of sweat glands, most notably in hidradenitis suppurativa.
Irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem function, with absent reflexes and apnea, while the heart may continue beating.
A benign liver mass from hyperplastic response to a vascular malformation. It has a central stellate scar and is not tied to oral contraceptives.
Tumors arising from trophoblast, including hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma. They produce high hCG.
An antiprotozoal used for Pneumocystis pneumonia and trypanosomiasis. Toxicities include pancreatitis, hypoglycemia and nephrotoxicity.
A rapidly fatal infection by Naegleria fowleri, a free-living amoeba entering through the nose from warm freshwater. It destroys the olfactory bulbs and brain.
The enzyme that converts HIV RNA into DNA. It is the target of NRTIs and NNRTIs.
Cranial nerve VIII, which carries hearing and balance information. It runs through the internal acoustic meatus and is affected by schwannoma.
Brain structures lacking a blood-brain barrier, such as the area postrema, subfornical organ and OVLT. They sense blood osmolarity and toxins.
Slow, writhing involuntary movements of the fingers and limbs, seen in cerebral palsy and basal ganglia damage.
Stomach cells that secrete histamine in response to gastrin, stimulating parietal cells to secrete acid.
A break of the proximal femur, such as a femoral neck, intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric fracture, common in elderly osteoporotic patients. Femoral neck fractures risk avascular necrosis.
A bulk-forming fiber laxative from plantago seeds, used for constipation and mild lowering of cholesterol.
An opioid antidiarrheal that slows gut motility, combined with atropine to discourage abuse.
A hepatitis C antiviral that inhibits NS5B RNA polymerase. It is used in combination regimens to cure infection.
A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor used for HIV and hepatitis B.
A kinase that phosphorylates and activates MAP kinase in the RAS-MAPK pathway. MEK is its main example.
A system in which blood passes through two capillary beds in series. The hepatic portal system and the hypothalamic-pituitary portal system are examples.
Opioid peptides made in the pituitary and brain from proopiomelanocortin. They reduce pain and produce euphoria.
A peptide from POMC that increases melanin production in melanocytes. Excess ACTH can darken skin through it.
Anterior pituitary cells secreting LH and FSH in response to GnRH.
Anterior pituitary cells that secrete TSH in response to TRH.
The energy used at rest to maintain basic body functions, raised by thyroid hormone.
The middle adrenal cortex layer, making cortisol under ACTH stimulation.
Urinary metabolites of androgens made in the adrenals and gonads. Elevated levels suggest adrenal androgen excess.
Hormones secreted by fat cells, such as leptin and adiponectin, regulating appetite and insulin sensitivity.
A potent intravenous bisphosphonate that inhibits osteoclasts. It treats osteoporosis, Paget disease and hypercalcemia of malignancy, with osteonecrosis of the jaw as a risk.
Bone disease from hyperparathyroidism, with osteoclastic resorption, brown tumors and cysts.
A U-shaped bone in the neck that supports the tongue and larynx. It is the only bone not articulating with another bone.
A congenital neck cyst from remnants of the branchial apparatus, usually along the anterior sternocleidomastoid.
A large glycosaminoglycan in connective tissue, joint fluid and vitreous that holds water and lubricates.
An MHC class I allele associated with faster progression of HIV.
A benign tumor of the parathyroid gland, the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism. It causes hypercalcemia, kidney stones and bone disease.
A membrane transporter exchanging intracellular H+ for extracellular Na+, regulating pH in the proximal tubule.
Narrowing of arteries in the limbs, usually from atherosclerosis. It causes claudication and rest pain.
Contractile cells wrapped around capillaries that regulate flow and support the blood-brain barrier.
A mutation in egg or sperm cells that is heritable and present in every cell of offspring.
Anterior rami of thoracic spinal nerves running between ribs, supplying chest wall muscles and skin.
Abnormally short stature, most commonly achondroplasia from an FGFR3 mutation.
Inherited syndromes of tumors in several endocrine glands. MEN1 involves pituitary, parathyroid and pancreas; MEN2 involves medullary thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma.
A liver cytochrome P450 enzyme that metabolizes warfarin, phenytoin and NSAIDs. Genetic variants slow warfarin clearance.
A DPP-4 inhibitor that increases incretin levels, raising insulin and lowering glucagon in type 2 diabetes. It is weight neutral and risks pancreatitis.
Sugars made of two monosaccharides, such as sucrose, lactose and maltose. Disaccharidases in the brush border split them.
Stem cells in seminiferous tubules that divide to form primary spermatocytes.
Having a single set of chromosomes, as in egg and sperm cells (23 in humans).
Complete absence of sperm in semen, caused by testicular failure or obstruction.
A procedure that destroys the endometrium to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding.
A synthetic estrogen given to pregnant women, causing clear cell vaginal adenocarcinoma and structural genital anomalies in daughters.
A cancer with cells rich in glycogen appearing clear. It occurs in the vagina after DES exposure and in the kidney and ovary.
Drugs acting as estrogen agonists in some tissues and antagonists in others, such as tamoxifen and raloxifene.
A mass of normal tissue in an abnormal location, such as gastric tissue in a Meckel diverticulum.
The transitional epithelium lining the renal pelvis, ureters and bladder. It stretches and is the origin of urothelial carcinoma.
A hydatidiform mole that invades the myometrium and may metastasize. It retains villi and is treated with chemotherapy.
A prostate cancer grading system based on glandular architecture, scored from patterns 1-5 and summed.
A nonsteroidal antiandrogen that blocks androgen receptors, used in prostate cancer. It can cause hepatotoxicity.
Compounds mimicking pyrophosphate, such as bisphosphonates and foscarnet, which block bone resorption or viral DNA polymerase.
Inflammation of the esophagus from acid reflux, causing heartburn and risk of strictures and Barrett esophagus.
Glucose stored as glycogen in the liver, broken down between meals to maintain blood sugar.
